_note: The verdict: what Cockpit checks about a turn on a ticket after the rescan settles (engine/verify.js). Each check is one question; the wording here is what the ticket page shows; on=false leaves it out; blocks=false makes it a warning that cannot hold the ticket in work. gate: ticket - asked of every turn on a ticket (its verdict); promote - the environment, asked of the whole project before anything is promoted (the Tests tab). The built-in checks are measured by the engine; a check you add is one of three kinds - problem (a Problems rule that must not fire on the ticket's files), command (a command run in the project folder after the turn that must exit 0), pattern (a regular expression that must not appear in the touched files). Edited from Settings › Plugins and cards › Tickets, or here; read on every verdict, no restart.

checks.name: findings on the scope
checks.asks: Did the turn leave the ticket's files with no more Problems findings than before?
checks.why: The 91 Problems rules run over the whole project on every scan; this counts the ones that land on the ticket's declared files, before the turn and after. The work may fix findings; it may not add any.
checks.measures: the number of Problems tags on the declared files, before → after; up is red, and the detail names the rules that fired
checks.fix: open Problems, filter to the ticket's files, and have the AI clear what it added - or send the ticket round again

checks.name: no new shape break
checks.asks: Did the turn add a structural break - a screen touching data, SQL in an action, a write across features?
checks.why: The shape rules (screen-touches-data, sql-in-action, data-reaches-up, cross-feature-write, action-calls-action, logic-serves-screen, skips-logic) are the ones that outweigh ten style findings: they are how a codebase stops being readable.
checks.measures: the number of shape-rule tags on the declared files, before → after
checks.fix: the detail names the rule; the fix is moving the code to the layer it belongs in, never silencing the rule

checks.name: coverage not down
checks.asks: Are as many of the ticket's files named by a passing test as before?
checks.why: A turn that breaks or deletes a test quietly lowers the floor under everything after it.
checks.measures: of the declared files, how many a passing test names, before → after
checks.fix: restore or repair the test the turn broke; a file that lost its test needs one before the ticket passes

checks.name: no new AI slop in the touched files
checks.asks: Did the turn leave the marks AI code leaves - empty catches, fake success, TODO stubs, debug logging, commented-out code, unbounded queries, string-built SQL, eval?
checks.why: These are the findings an AI adds most and a person notices least. Every touched file is looked at, declared or not.
checks.measures: the slop-rule tags on every touched file after the turn that were not there before
checks.fix: the detail names the file and the rule; have the AI clean it in the same ticket

checks.name: the project's tests pass
checks.asks: Did the project's own test run pass after the turn - and does the project have tests at all?
checks.why: Cockpit runs the tests after every turn (engine/tests.js). A project with no tests cannot be verified: nothing proves the work. The first ticket on a new project is to write them.
checks.measures: the latest test report: at least one test, none failed, the test database setup ok
checks.fix: read the failing test in the detail; the AI fixes the code, never the test, unless the ticket says the test was wrong. No tests: a ticket to write them.

checks.name: every flow is proven by a test
checks.asks: Does each declared flow have a passing test that names it?
checks.why: A flow (## Flows in a feature README) is what the product promises; a test that names it is the proof. An unproven flow is a promise nobody checked.
checks.measures: the flows on the map against the tests that name them and passed in the last run (flow-without-test, flow-failing)
checks.fix: declare the flows, write the test that names each, or fix the one that fails

checks.name: the app starts and answers
checks.asks: Did the app come up under the runner and answer on its routes?
checks.why: Every later check (contract, sign-in, DAST) needs a running app. A project that cannot be started by a machine cannot be tested by one.
checks.measures: the app stage of the test run: started from start: under ## Tests, answering at url:, routes probed
checks.fix: add start: and url: under ## Tests in project.md; if it started and died, the detail says why

checks.name: the routes keep their contract
checks.asks: Do the routes still answer with the shape they answered with before?
checks.why: The recorded shape of each route's answer is the contract the front end and other callers rely on; a changed field is a break nobody announced.
checks.measures: the contract stage: each probed route's JSON shape against the recorded one
checks.fix: the detail names the route and the field; either the change was meant (the ticket says so; re-record) or it is a break to fix

checks.name: DAST finds nothing high
checks.asks: Did the last dynamic security scan (ZAP) of the running app finish clean of high-risk alerts, within the week?
checks.why: DAST is the outside view: what an attacker sees. A high alert is a door open to the internet. Warns by default: a private site fixes what it finds without every promote waiting on a scan; a project may set it to block.
checks.measures: the latest DAST run: finished, no high-risk alerts, not older than 7 days
checks.fix: the alert names the route and the risk; fix it and run DAST again from the Tests tab

checks.name: the migrations cycle
checks.asks: Do the database migrations go up and down clean on the test database?
checks.why: A migration that cannot be reversed is a deploy that cannot be rolled back.
checks.measures: the setup stage of the test run: up, down, up on the *_test database (only when db/migrations exists)
checks.fix: write the .down.sql the detail names, or fix the one that fails

checks.name: the sign-in works and doors hold
checks.asks: Can the runner sign in as the declared user, and do the doors answer as declared?
checks.why: Doors behind a login are unproven until something signs in and tries them.
checks.measures: the signed-in stage: login: and user: under ## Tests, each route's answer against its declared access (login-failed, door-refuses-user)
checks.fix: declare login: and user: under ## Tests; the detail names the door that refused or opened wrongly

checks.name: backup and restore proven
checks.asks: Can the database be backed up and restored, and is the backup fresh?
checks.why: A backup that was never restored is a hope, not a backup.
checks.measures: the restore drill on the *_test database (scripts/backup.js, scripts/restore.js) and the backup folder's age (only when there is a database)
checks.fix: the detail says which step failed or what is missing

checks.name: the work is committed
checks.asks: Is every file the ticket names and the turn touched committed in git?
checks.why: The promote moves commits, never loose files; uncommitted work would be verified here and missing in prod.
checks.measures: git status on the declared and touched files: nothing modified, added or deleted uncommitted
checks.fix: have the AI commit its work naming the ticket (every commit names it), or commit it yourself

checks.name: every touched file was declared
checks.asks: Did the turn stay inside the files the ticket named?
checks.why: The ticket's files are its blast radius - what you approved, what the impact was computed on. A file touched outside them is work nobody approved.
checks.measures: the files the turn touched (from the AI's own file events) against the ticket's alter + create + delete lists; the detail names the undeclared ones
checks.fix: if the extra files were right, the ticket should have named them - fix the ticket's files; if they were not, have the AI revert them

checks.name: every declared file was touched
checks.asks: Did the turn do all of what the ticket named?
checks.why: A declared file the turn never touched is either work left undone or a ticket that named too much; either way the ticket and the work disagree.
checks.measures: the ticket's alter + create + delete lists against the files the turn touched; the detail names the untouched ones
checks.fix: send it round again for the rest, or take the file off the ticket if it was never needed

checks.name: nothing deleted that the ticket did not name
checks.asks: Did the turn remove a file nobody asked it to remove?
checks.why: Deleting is work, so it is declared. A cleanup command that takes what it was not pointed at - git clean, rm -rf on a directory, a pasted path - destroys files no ticket asked about and no commit explains (2026-09-22: 97 test files, and a project's whole .cockpit folder, in one night).
checks.measures: git's deletions since the ticket's work began (committed, staged and unstaged) against the ticket's --delete list; Cockpit's own folder is never judged
checks.fix: put them back - git checkout -- <path> - or, if the deletion was right, add them to the ticket with `ticket edit --delete`

checks.name: the ticket's flow clicks through
checks.asks: Does the flow this ticket is part of work in a real browser, on dev, now?
checks.why: A ticket names the README flow it belongs to (--flow); its browser test is written first and goes red, the code makes it green. Green here is the proof a person can do the thing - not that the code runs.
checks.measures: the flow named on the ticket has a *.browser.test.js naming it (@flow) that passed in the latest test run; a ticket with no flow is green here only when it names --flow none with a reason on the ticket
checks.fix: write the browser flow test for the flow (test/<feature>.<flow>.browser.test.js, require(process.env.COCKPIT_FLOW)), run the tests, read the screenshot on red
